subject: Cloud Computing
title: Single Sign-On for Cloud
description: A short lesson to help you apply Single Sign-On for Cloud.

hook.text: Your company uses 100 SaaS tools. Without SSO, that's 100 separate passwords per employee.

buildup.text: Single Sign-On lets users log in once and access many applications. One identity, many services.

discovery.text: Providers like Okta and Azure AD federate identity across cloud apps using protocols like SAML and OIDC.

twist.text: SSO is a single point of failure. If the identity provider goes down, nobody can log into anything.

climax.text: SSO reduces password fatigue and improves security. But it demands that the identity provider is rock-solid.

punchline.text: One login for everything. Protect that one login with your life.

quiz.question: What is a risk of relying on Single Sign-On?
options: If the identity provider goes down, access to all connected services is lost
SSO requires users to remember more passwords than before
Only one user can be logged in at a time across the company

details.summary: SSO lets users authenticate once and access multiple cloud services without re-entering credentials. It centralizes identity management, reduces password fatigue, and makes it easier to enforce consistent security policies across all connected applications.
details.whyItMatters: Without SSO, employees manage dozens of passwords, increasing the risk of weak or reused credentials. Centralized authentication improves both security and user experience.
takeaways: Users authenticate once to access multiple services
Centralizes identity management and policy enforcement
Reduces password fatigue and reuse across applications

faq.question: What protocols power SSO?
faq.answer: SAML 2.0 and OpenID Connect are the most common protocols. SAML is widely used in enterprise environments, while OIDC built on OAuth 2.0 is more modern and popular with web and mobile applications. Both enable federated identity across services.

faq.question: Does SSO create a single point of failure?
faq.answer: If the identity provider goes down, users cannot authenticate to any connected service. Organizations mitigate this with high-availability identity provider configurations, cached sessions, and emergency break-glass accounts with separate credentials.
